questions.stem: An HR operations coordinator wants to bring Claude into the company's employee-onboarding process, which currently has four manual steps: (1) chasing new hires for completed forms, (2) writing a personalized welcome email and first-week schedule for each new hire, (3) checking right-to-work documents, and (4) approving equipment requests that exceed the standard budget. About 30 people start each month. Which step is the BEST place to start augmenting with Claude?

options.text: Checking right-to-work documents, because Claude can read document files faster than a coordinator can review them by hand.
Approving over-budget equipment requests, because Claude applies the budget policy more consistently than any individual manager.
Drafting the welcome emails and first-week schedules, which the coordinator reviews and edits before anything is sent.
All four steps at once in a single detailed prompt, so the team sees the largest possible saving in coordinator hours.

questions.explanation: A good first integration point is **high-volume, template-like work whose output a person can check quickly** before it goes out. Welcome emails and schedules fit: the coordinator knows what a correct one looks like, mistakes are cheap to catch, and the work repeats every month. This augments one step while the rest of the process and its owners stay unchanged.

whyWrong.A: Right-to-work checks carry legal weight and depend on judging whether a document is genuine and acceptable. Reading speed is not the deciding factor, so this is a poor first step to hand to Claude.
whyWrong.B: Approving budget exceptions is a judgment call with financial impact. Claude can summarize a request, but the approval should stay with an accountable person.
whyWrong.D: Changing every step at once gives you no evidence about where Claude is reliable, and it pulls the high-stakes steps in with the easy ones.

questions.mindset: Start where output is frequent, low-stakes and easy for a human to check.

questions.stem: A finance team has used Claude for one quarter to draft the monthly variance commentary that analysts then check and edit. The head of finance now wonders whether to redesign the whole month-end reporting process around Claude, not just speed up drafting. Which TWO observations are the STRONGEST reasons to consider a redesign? Choose TWO.

options.text: A vendor demo showed an end-to-end tool that writes the commentary and sends it straight to executives with no reviewer involved.
A 90-minute monthly meeting exists mainly so managers can hear analysts read out summaries of reports nobody had time to read.
Leadership wants a visible AI success story to announce at the company-wide meeting scheduled for the end of this month.
Three months of review logs show analysts' corrections to Claude's drafts are few, minor and stable from month to month.
The first two drafts Claude produced during initial testing were praised by the CFO for their clarity and structure.

questions.explanation: Redesign makes sense when (1) a step exists **mainly because something used to be expensive**, such as reading and summarizing, and Claude makes that cheap, and (2) you have **evidence from augmenting** that Claude is reliable for this work. The meeting that only relays summaries is a candidate for rethinking. A quarter of stable correction data is the evidence that justifies a bigger change.

whyWrong.A: A demo of a tool that removes reviewers is not evidence about your process. Sending executive reporting with no human check also drops a key control.
whyWrong.C: Wanting a visible win is a political motive, not a sign that the process is ready to change. Redesigns driven by announcements tend to skip measurement.
whyWrong.E: Two praised drafts is anecdote, not evidence. Reliability shows up across many months of real cases, including hard ones.

questions.mindset: Redesign steps that exist because work used to be costly, and only once augmentation has produced evidence.

questions.stem: A legal-operations team has used Claude for four months to summarize incoming NDAs, and a paralegal reviews every summary before it goes to the business requester. The review log shows median review time has fallen from nine minutes to under a minute, corrections have dropped to zero, and last week a counterparty pointed out a wrong term length in a summary that had been approved. What is the MOST effective response?

options.text: Add a short checklist of the facts the paralegal must verify, spot-check a random sample of approved summaries, and track any escaped errors.
Add an instruction telling Claude to double-check every summary for errors before showing it, so the paralegal has less to catch.
Move NDA summaries to the most capable Claude model available, since a stronger model should make far fewer mistakes like this.
Require the paralegal to rewrite every summary from scratch from the NDA itself, so nothing Claude produces is relied upon.

questions.explanation: These are the signs of the **rubber-stamp trap**: the review still exists on paper, but reviewers approve without reading. The fix is to make review real again: a short checklist of the facts that must be verified (parties, term, governing law), random spot checks of approved items, and tracking of corrections and **escaped errors**. These keep the human checkpoint working without throwing away the time saved.

whyWrong.B: Asking Claude to check itself does not fix a human review that has stopped working. The escaped error got through the reviewer, and that is the control that needs repair.
whyWrong.C: A stronger model may reduce errors but cannot remove them, and it does nothing about reviewers who have stopped reading.
whyWrong.D: Rewriting everything from scratch throws away the benefit of the workflow. The problem is review quality, not the existence of drafts.

questions.mindset: A checkpoint only counts if people actually check; watch for review times and corrections falling to zero.

questions.stem: In a billing-dispute workflow, a finance analyst uses a Claude Project to draft a dispute summary with a proposed credit amount, then forwards it to the account manager, who sends the reply to the customer. Twice this month, a wrong credit amount reached a customer. In both cases the analyst assumed the account manager would check the figures, and the account manager assumed the analyst already had. What is the BEST fix with minimal disruption?

options.text: Add a second Claude step that re-reads each draft and confirms the credit amount is correct before it is forwarded.
Add a line to every customer email noting that the credit figures were prepared with AI assistance and may contain errors.
Ask both the analyst and the account manager to give every summary a complete, independent review before it is sent.
Name one owner, the analyst, who must verify the credit amount against the billing system and record that check before forwarding.

questions.explanation: The failure is a **hand-off with no clear owner**: each person thought the other was the checkpoint. The fix is to name one accountable person for the specific check (figures against the billing system of record) and record that it was done. "Someone will look at it" is not a control. A named owner with a defined check is.

whyWrong.A: Having Claude check Claude does not verify the numbers against the billing system, and it still leaves no person accountable for the figure.
whyWrong.B: A disclaimer pushes the risk onto the customer and does nothing to stop wrong credits being sent.
whyWrong.C: Two full reviews double the effort and can still leave each reviewer relying on the other. Shared responsibility is the cause here, not the fix.

questions.mindset: Every checkpoint needs a named owner and a defined check, especially at hand-offs.

questions.stem: A customer-support team lead plans to redesign how her team handles warranty requests, with Claude doing much of the reading and drafting. She has a strong sense of where time is wasted but nothing written down. What is the BEST first step?

options.text: Write a detailed prompt for the warranty replies right away, since the first drafts will show where the process should change.
Map the current process with the people who do it, including hand-offs and checks, and record baseline time and error figures.
Announce the new Claude-based process to the whole team, so that everyone can start using it from next Monday morning.
Ask Claude to design the ideal warranty process from scratch, and adopt its proposal as the team's new standard operating procedure.

questions.explanation: You cannot redesign well, or prove improvement, without knowing how the work runs today. Mapping the current process **with the people who do it** shows the real steps, hand-offs and checks (including the ones that matter for quality). A **baseline** of time and errors lets you show later whether the change helped.

whyWrong.A: Starting with a prompt optimizes one step before you know which steps matter, and without a baseline you cannot show any gain.
whyWrong.C: Announcing a new process before it is designed or tested skips discovery, measurement and buy-in, which are the parts that make adoption stick.
whyWrong.D: Claude can help sketch options, but a design made without the team's knowledge of real exceptions and controls should not be adopted unchecked.

questions.mindset: Map the current process and measure a baseline before changing it.

questions.stem: Every Friday an operations coordinator opens twelve team update documents in Google Drive, copies their contents into a Claude chat, and asks for a one-page status digest, which she checks before emailing it to department heads. The copying takes about an hour. Her organization's admins have already approved and enabled the Google Drive connector for her plan. What is the BEST improvement?

options.text: Use the approved Google Drive connector so Claude can read the update documents directly, and keep checking the digest before it is emailed.
Export the twelve documents and upload them each week to her personal Claude account, which she finds quicker to use than the company workspace.
Ask the internal developer team to build a custom integration that pulls the twelve update documents into Claude every Friday.
Keep copying the twelve documents in by hand, but split them across several smaller chats so each response comes back faster.

questions.explanation: When an **approved connector** already exists for the tool the work lives in, using it removes the copy-and-paste step without any new build. The coordinator's check before sending stays in place, because the digest goes to department heads.

whyWrong.B: Moving company documents into a personal account bypasses approved tools and data policy, whatever the convenience.
whyWrong.C: A custom build is over-engineering when an approved connector already does the job. Developer time should go to needs that chat features cannot meet.
whyWrong.D: Splitting chats keeps the slow manual copying step and makes it harder for Claude to combine the updates into one consistent digest.

questions.mindset: Use approved, built-in connections to existing tools before asking for custom builds.

questions.stem: A marketing team now uses Claude to draft product-page copy, cutting drafting time from about three hours to twenty minutes per page. Because drafting is now cheap, the number of pages requested each week has roughly tripled, and every page still requires compliance approval before publication. The compliance review queue has grown from about 10 to 35 pages a week, and the average time from request to published page has not changed. What should the team do NEXT to improve the workflow?

options.text: Ask the compliance reviewers to work through their queue of drafts more quickly, since Claude-written copy is tidy and consistent.
Have Claude pre-check drafts against compliance's checklist and flag likely issues, with reviewers still approving every page.
Let pages that Claude itself rates as low-risk skip compliance review entirely, so the queue shrinks to the pages needing it.
Move drafting to a faster, cheaper Claude model so pages enter the compliance queue even sooner than they do today.

questions.explanation: Making one step cheap raised throughput and pushed the constraint **downstream to compliance review**. Integration has to be judged on the **whole workflow**, not on the step you changed. Using Claude to support the constrained step — a pre-check against compliance's own checklist that flags likely issues — helps reviewers work faster while compliance keeps the approval decision. Measuring end-to-end cycle time then shows whether the change worked.

whyWrong.A: Asking reviewers to work faster weakens the control. That is how the rubber-stamp trap starts.
whyWrong.C: Letting Claude decide which pages skip a required compliance approval removes a human checkpoint on public, regulated content.
whyWrong.D: Faster drafting adds to the queue that is already the constraint, so the time to publish will not improve.

questions.mindset: Measure the whole workflow; speeding one step can just push the bottleneck downstream.

questions.stem: A trade association sends a monthly newsletter on regulatory changes to about 40,000 members. The workflow is: a researcher gathers sources on recent changes, Claude drafts the articles, a designer lays out the issue as an Artifact, and the issue is sent to members. Where should the association place named human checkpoints? Choose TWO.

options.text: A subject expert verifies the regulatory claims, dates and figures in the draft against the researcher's primary sources.
A staff member approves each individual search query the researcher runs before it is allowed to fetch any source material.
A named editor gives final sign-off on the complete issue, once it is laid out, before it is sent to all members.
A designer reviews whether the Artifact's colors match the association's official brand palette before anything else happens.
Claude rates its own confidence in each paragraph, and any paragraph scored as highly confident skips the expert check.

questions.explanation: Put checkpoints **where an error would be costly**: content with regulatory weight going to a large external audience. An expert verifying claims against the cited primary sources catches hallucinated or misread details. A named editor's final sign-off ensures one person owns what is published.

whyWrong.B: Approving each search query adds friction at a low-risk point. What matters is checking the claims in the output, not policing every search.
whyWrong.D: A brand-color check may be good practice, but it is not where costly errors happen, so it is not one of the critical checkpoints.
whyWrong.E: Claude's confidence rating is not verification. Letting it decide what skips the expert check removes the control where it is needed most.

questions.mindset: Place named human checkpoints where errors are expensive: external, regulated, high-reach outputs.

questions.stem: An IT support team has redesigned its morning routine. Instead of agents skimming the overnight escalation queue, one agent asks Claude in the team's Project to summarize and categorize all new escalations, and the team works from that list. It has saved about an hour a day for two months. Before the manager calls the redesign finished, what is the MOST important gap to close?

options.text: Upgrade every team member to the highest available plan so that usage limits can never again interrupt the morning summary.
Keep both the manual skim and the Claude summary running every morning permanently, so the two lists can always be compared.
Write down a fallback procedure for when Claude is unavailable or limits are reached, and keep a regular sample check of categorizations.
Ask Claude to add a confidence score to each category, so the team can skip checking anything it rates as highly confident.

questions.explanation: A redesigned process now **depends** on Claude, so it needs **continuity and ongoing quality checks**. A documented fallback (who triages manually, and how) keeps work moving during an outage or when usage limits are reached. A regular sample check catches drift in categorization before urgent escalations get mis-sorted.

whyWrong.A: A bigger plan may raise limits, but it does not guarantee availability and it is a cost decision, not a continuity plan.
whyWrong.B: Running both processes forever removes the time saved. A fallback that can be switched on, plus sample checks, gives the same protection at far lower cost.
whyWrong.D: Claude's own confidence is not a reliable check, and skipping review on that basis weakens the very quality control the redesign needs.

questions.mindset: A redesigned workflow needs a fallback and ongoing checks, not just a good first month.

questions.stem: A consultancy rolled out a Claude Project to help consultants draft client proposals. After six weeks, only 4 of 15 consultants use it. The others say the drafts "don't sound like us" and that they are unsure which part of the proposal process it is meant for. Which TWO actions are MOST likely to improve adoption while keeping quality? Choose TWO.

options.text: Make use of the Project mandatory for the whole team, and report each consultant's weekly prompt count as a performance metric.
Retire the proposal workflow now, because low adoption after six weeks shows the team does not really need Claude for this work.
Collect drafts that consultants rejected, and update the Project's instructions and examples to match the firm's house voice.
Replace the Project with a more capable Claude model, because better writing on its own will persuade the consultants to switch.
Have early users show colleagues which step they use it for and how they check the output, then add these to the playbook.

questions.explanation: The non-users gave two specific reasons, so fix both. **Voice**: real rejected drafts show exactly what to change in the Project's instructions and example files — concrete examples shape output more reliably than abstract instructions alone. **Clarity of use**: peers showing which step they use it for and how they verify the output, written into the playbook, makes the workflow concrete and keeps the review habit.

whyWrong.A: Mandates and prompt counts drive empty usage, not good proposals, and they ignore the reasons people gave for not using it.
whyWrong.B: Low early adoption with clear, fixable reasons is a signal to adjust, not proof that the use case fails.
whyWrong.D: Model choice is not the stated problem. Without the firm's voice in the instructions and examples, any model will still sound generic.

questions.mindset: Adoption follows fit and clarity: fix the reasons people give, and spread working practice peer to peer.

questions.stem: A corporate legal team's contract-intake process works well and meets its turnaround targets. The one slow step is writing a plain-language summary of each contract for the business person who requested it, which takes lawyers about 40 minutes per contract. A colleague proposes rebuilding the entire intake process around Claude. What is the MOST appropriate approach?

options.text: Rebuild the whole intake process around Claude now, since a full redesign will capture far more value than changing one step.
Leave the current intake process completely unchanged, because the risk of an error in a legal summary outweighs any time saved on drafting.
Have Claude draft the summaries with no lawyer review at all, because a plain-language summary is not formal legal advice.
Use Claude to draft the plain-language summaries, with a lawyer checking each before it goes out, and measure the time saved.

questions.explanation: When a process **works and has one slow step**, the right move is usually to **augment** that step rather than redesign everything. Claude drafts the summary, a lawyer checks it (because the business acts on it), and measuring time saved gives evidence for any bigger change later.

whyWrong.A: Redesigning a working process with no evidence adds risk and change effort for no clear gain. Augment first, then redesign if the data supports it.
whyWrong.B: The risk of an error is real, which is exactly why the reviewed-drafting option keeps a lawyer in the loop rather than rejecting the change outright.
whyWrong.C: Business decisions rely on these summaries, so mistakes are costly. Removing the lawyer's check drops the control where it matters.

questions.mindset: If the process works and one step is slow, augment that step before redesigning anything.

questions.stem: A due-diligence team at a consulting firm wants to redesign its workflow so that Claude reads the documents in each client's data room and drafts the first-pass risk summary. The documents are covered by client confidentiality agreements. What should the team lead do BEFORE building the new workflow?

options.text: Build and launch the new data-room workflow first, and then remove client names from the documents later if anyone raises a concern about it.
Confirm that the client agreements and data policy allow these documents in the approved workspace, and agree what may be included.
Use personal Claude accounts for the client documents so that they are kept entirely apart from the company's own internal data.
Ask Claude in a general chat whether processing a client's documents would be permitted under a typical confidentiality agreement.

questions.explanation: Integrating Claude into a workflow that handles **confidential third-party data** starts with confirming that the data may be processed there: check client agreements and company policy, use only the **approved workspace**, and agree what may be included. Doing this first avoids a redesign that has to be torn down or, worse, a breach.

whyWrong.A: Fixing data handling after launch means confidential documents may already have been processed improperly. The check has to come first.
whyWrong.C: Personal accounts are outside company controls and are the opposite of keeping client data safe.
whyWrong.D: Whether the firm may process the documents depends on the actual agreements and policy, and the people accountable for them must confirm it. Claude's general view is not that confirmation.

questions.mindset: Confirm data permissions and approved tools before redesigning a workflow around sensitive data.

questions.stem: An insurer's customer-service agents review every Claude-drafted reply before it is sent. The team manager wants to move one category, confirmations of completed address updates, from 100% review to reviewing a random sample. Which TWO conditions BEST justify this change? Choose TWO.

options.text: Several months of review logs show near-zero substantive corrections in this category, and escaped errors are tracked as well.
Claude reports high confidence in its drafts for this category whenever the agents ask it to rate their own accuracy.
Agents have said in team meetings that reviewing these short confirmation messages is the most tedious part of their working day.
The category is agreed in policy to be low-risk: a mistake is easy to correct and carries no financial or legal consequence.
Competitors are reported to send AI-written customer messages to their own clients with no human review at any stage.

questions.explanation: Reducing review should rest on **evidence and risk**, not convenience. Months of logged data with near-zero corrections (and tracked escaped errors) show Claude is reliable for this category. A policy decision that the category is **low-risk and easy to reverse** shows a missed error would be cheap. Together they justify sampling, and the sampling keeps a check in place.

whyWrong.B: Claude's self-reported confidence is not evidence of accuracy, so it cannot justify relaxing review.
whyWrong.C: Reviewer boredom is a real signal for workflow design, but it says nothing about whether errors would get through.
whyWrong.E: What competitors do is not evidence about your error rate or your risk tolerance.

questions.mindset: Relax review only for low-risk categories, and only with logged evidence, never on confidence or convenience.

questions.stem: An internal audit team uses Claude to pre-screen about 3,000 expense reports a month against the travel policy. Claude flags roughly 150, and auditors review each flagged report and decide on any action. Since the change, auditors look only at flagged reports. What is the MOST important gap in this workflow?

options.text: No one checks the unflagged reports, so missed violations go unseen. Auditors should review a random sample of unflagged reports regularly.
Auditors still spend time on flagged reports. Claude should reject clear violations automatically so they handle only borderline cases.
Claude's flags are too brief. Each flag should include a longer written explanation so auditors can make faster decisions.
Claude should be told to flag far more reports, because a larger flagged set guarantees that no violation is ever missed.

questions.explanation: When Claude **triages**, human review often covers only what it flags. That checks false alarms but not **misses**. Sampling unflagged reports measures how many violations Claude lets through, which is the number that shows whether the screening can be trusted. Auditors still make every decision on flagged items.

whyWrong.B: Auto-rejection turns Claude's flag into the decision. That replaces auditor judgment on matters that affect employees.
whyWrong.C: Longer explanations may help with flagged items, but they do nothing about violations that were never flagged.
whyWrong.D: Flagging more increases auditor workload and still does not measure misses. No threshold "guarantees" completeness, and only checking unflagged items shows what is missed.

questions.mindset: When Claude filters work, check what it lets through, not just what it flags.

questions.stem: A payroll help desk answers employee questions by hand. The team lead has built a Claude Project containing the payroll policies and wants agents to send Claude-drafted answers after review. Before switching over, what is the MOST reliable way to validate the new workflow?

options.text: Test the Project on the ten example questions that were used to write its instructions, and switch over if all ten are answered correctly.
Switch the help desk over straight away, and fix the Project's instructions whenever an employee complains about an incorrect answer.
Run Claude drafts alongside the team's manual answers on the same real questions for two weeks, then judge against agreed criteria.
Ask Claude to estimate its own accuracy on payroll questions, and switch over if its estimate sits above the team's target accuracy.

questions.explanation: A **parallel run** on **real, current questions** mirrors the actual workload, including hard or unusual cases, and gives direct evidence of accuracy without exposing employees to risk. Logging the differences and deciding against **criteria agreed in advance** turns the switch into an evidence-based decision rather than a judgment call.

whyWrong.A: Questions used to build the instructions are the easiest possible test. They say little about the real, varied distribution of questions.
whyWrong.B: Waiting for complaints exposes employees to wrong pay information and only catches errors that people happen to notice.
whyWrong.D: Claude cannot reliably measure its own accuracy, so a self-estimate is not validation.

questions.mindset: Validate a new workflow on real cases, run side by side with the current one, against criteria agreed in advance.
